quote: Damit hängt eng die Frage zusammen, ob man nicht, wenn man bloss die Euklidische Geometrie aufbauen will, gleich von vornherein [-I-] Gruppe I, II, III nehmen soll und dann die [-Con-] Congruenzsätze in folgender Weise
english: Closely connected with this is the question whether, if one only wants to build up Euclidean geometry, one should not take groups I, II, III right from the start and then the congruence theorems in the following way
topic: Notes on proving Pascal's theorem and on structuring the axioms of Euclidean geometry with congruence theorems, then a derivation of commutativity of addition from the two distributive laws, and the start of a construction of a fourth-order surface with 10 closed sheets.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't a research problem. It's a choice about how to arrange the axioms. The question is whether a treatment aimed only at Euclidean geometry should state axiom groups I, II and III at the start and only then bring in congruence. In Hilbert's 1899 numbering these groups are incidence/connection (I), order (II) and the Euclidean parallel axiom in Playfair form (III). Assuming the notebook uses that numbering, putting the parallel axiom first lets the congruence theorems be developed more simply, inside the Euclidean setting. The sentence on the page breaks off before saying what 'in the following way' means, so the planned method for congruence can't be identified. The reading of 'III' as the parallel axiom is an inference from Hilbert's 1899 numbering, not something the page says.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert himself, in practice. The first edition of Grundlagen der Geometrie (Festschrift for Gauss and Weber, 1899), built on his Göttingen lectures from 1894 to 1898, orders the axioms I connection, II order, III parallels, IV congruence, V continuity. It says that introducing the parallel axiom 'simplifies greatly' the foundations. Later editions moved congruence up to III and parallels to IV. That move suits a neutral geometry that also covers non-Euclidean cases, so the parallels-first order is the one for 'Euclidean geometry only'. The surviving lecture notes are edited in Hallett & Majer (eds.), David Hilbert's Lectures on the Foundations of Geometry 1891–1902 (Springer, 2004).

evidence.claim: The English translation of the 1899 Grundlagen has Group III as the axiom of parallels (Euclid's axiom) and Group IV as the axioms of congruence. It says introducing the parallel axiom greatly simplifies the foundations.

The first edition of the Grundlagen was based on Hilbert's Göttingen lectures of 1894–1898 and appeared in 1899 in a Festschrift for Gauss and Weber. The source gives the later, well-known order of Incidence, Order, Congruence, Parallels, Continuity.
Hilbert's lecture notes on the foundations of geometry from 1891 to 1902, together with the 1899 first edition, are edited by Hallett and Majer.

triage.why: The note asks how best to organise an axiom system for Euclidean geometry. That's a methodological decision, not an open theorem, and it isn't one of the 23 problems or the 24th. Hilbert's own 1899 book adopts exactly this layout: incidence, order and parallels first, then congruence. So the question was settled when he chose that structure, and he later reordered the groups in subsequent editions. Confidence is only medium for three reasons. I haven't seen the page itself. The sentence is cut off before the congruence method is given. And I couldn't find a source that discusses this particular notebook entry; the link to the 1899 Festschrift comes from my comparison, not from a source that makes it.
